visible.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): capital metro — the entire scene (NGOs including MHOL), anonymity of 10 million; Miraflores/Barranco visitor districts experience a normal Latin-urban climate. Its own sources sharpen the picture: the Congressional Women and Family Committee unanimously approved bills barring trans people from public toilets of the sex assigned at birth (20 Feb 2025; the plenary approved the fused text on 2 April 2025, with custody, medical, caregiving and disability exceptions), and the international airport relabeled its bathrooms to "women in their diversity / men in their diversity" after a 2023 complaint. A university observatory counted 54 LGBTQ+ killings and 170 rights violations 2020-2023, 30 of the dead trans women; in Feb 2023 a 31-year-old trans sex worker was abducted from central Lima's Chancay street by a criminal gang and shot dead. Scored relative to the national score (0.36) for Peru.
visible.tangentialFactors: Gay men account for 23 of the 54 killings counted 2020-2023 — an LGB-specific violence pattern that shapes the security climate without being directed at gender expression as such.

sources.claim: Source for this record (national norm + Lima-city detail): Infobae (20 Feb 2025) reports the Congress Women and Family Commission unanimously approved the bill barring trans people from public bathrooms of the sex not matching their biological sex at birth; the text also obliges removal of “ambiguous” signage of the kind the international airport Jorge Chávez had placed (“for all persons with female identity” / “male identity”). Activist Gianna Camacho is quoted warning enforcement will amount to ID (DNI) checks by security staff judging who may enter a bathroom, which she calls discriminatory and based on prejudice.

Source for this record (capital-scene violence data): Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) reports the Observatory recorded 54 murders of TLGBI people and 170 reported rights violations in Peru 2020–2023, trans women the most affected (30 of 54 dead), 19 homicides in 2023, and no identified suspects in 26 killings. It names the 12 Feb 2023 “Los Gallegos” gang kidnapping of trans sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano (31) from jirón Chancay in central Lima, killed with roughly 30 gunshots, as an example of the capital pattern, and notes the state keeps no system recording sexual orientation in killings.

visible.summary:
Ankara is the administrative core of what the country's leading LGBTI rights organisation — reporting from its capital launch event in 2025 — documented as hostility turned into explicit state policy: presidency-centred targeting, the family ministry as implementing body, broadcast and platform censorship, an LGBTI organisation closed, six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated) with trans people most affected, and no official hate-crime statistics in existence. A leaked October 2025 judicial package would add up to three years' imprisonment for conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion, and bar gender-affirming care below age 25.

The capital hosts the machinery that drafts and enforces those measures; nothing on record shows local countervailing protection, and the same courts and ministries that field the report operate here.
visible.tangentialFactors: State penalties on LGBT-inclusive digital content and broadcasts (censorship, platform fines, broadcaster withdrawals) plus blanket event bans form a national hostility climate implemented locally, affecting queer visibility broadly rather than gender identity per se.
visible.localsOnly: The draft law package's gender-affirming care restrictions (minimum age 25, eligibility conditions) and national health-ministry trans-care rules bear on residents; visitors cannot obtain transition care here.

sources.claim: National-framework source (applies country-wide; the package is drafted and enforced by institutions operating in Ankara): HRW (29 Oct 2025) reports the leaked draft “11th Judicial Package” would amend the Turkish penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality with up to three years’ prison, participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals; healthcare professionals performing such interventions would face fines and up to seven years in prison, trans people receiving deemed-illegal care up to three years, and courts could order pretrial detention. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft.

National-framework monitoring report (the institutions it names — the presidency, the Ministry of Family — operate in Ankara): Kaos GL’s annual report (“The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People”, launched in 2025) finds LGBTI+ hostility became explicit state policy — hostility centered on the presidency, the Ministry of Family as implementing ministry, broadcasts censored and artistic events cancelled or banned, and an LGBTI+ association closed for the first time in years with criminal cases opened against 11 of its members. It documents six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated), trans people the most affected, a sharp rise in torture and ill-treatment violations (89 versus 51 the previous year), and notes the state keeps no official hate-crime statistics.

sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a leaked '11th Judicial Package' would amend the penal and civil codes with articles threatening LGBT people — behaviour 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' and its 'promotion' (up to three years' prison, amending the indecent-acts provision); sharp restrictions on gender-affirming care (minimum age 25, onerous eligibility); potential charges against trans people, care providers, civil-society organisations and journalists; justified as protecting 'the family and public morals'.

Wikipedia's country page on LGBT rights in Turkey is the framework under which Eskişehir stands, and it names the province directly: in June 2021 police blocked the first Eskişehir pride parade, showing that even in this university city local authorities have suppressed the local Pride event. On the national frame, homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision that was ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. It also records that Kadir Has University surveys saw public support for equal rights for LGBTQ people rise from 33% in 2016 to 45% in 2020.

Duvar English reports that days after police interventions in Istanbul and Ankara, Turkish police attacked Eskişehir's first planned Pride march: officers were on the scene hours before the scheduled meeting time conducting identity checks, organisers were not allowed to hold a press meeting or conduct the parade, and police detained 20 people on the grounds of 'violating the ban on the march'. The article notes Turkish authorities have repeatedly banned Pride events in recent years citing security concerns and public order. This is direct, locally specific evidence of how the national Pride-ban policy was enforced in Eskişehir itself, the key factual basis for this record's risk assessment.

visible.summary:
Gaziantep sits fully under the national framework with no documented local divergence in either direction: the leaked October 2025 judicial package would criminalise conduct contrary to biological sex and its promotion (up to three years) and restrict gender-affirming care to age 25 and above, while the 2025 national rights report documents hostility as explicit state policy — presidency-centred targeting, censorship, an organisation closed, six violations of the right to life with trans people most affected, and no official protection statistics at all.

Nothing in the record shows this province offering either special danger beyond, or protection beneath, that national baseline; a visibly trans visitor's exposure is the national one, locally enforced.

Wikipedia's country page on LGBT rights in Turkey is the framework under which Gaziantep stands, matching this record's premise that the province sits fully under the national baseline: homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858 and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988 (with surgery, medical examination and court permission), but there is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law and same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. Since 2015 authorities have banned Pride events in most years, and participants have faced police attacks; in ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Turkey placed 47th of 49 countries. In early 2026 Turkish media reported the government was considering legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex', a provision ultimately not included in that year's judicial reform package. The page records no Gaziantep-specific divergence, consistent with this record's assessment that a visibly trans visitor's exposure in the province is the national one, locally enforced.

Amnesty International's Türkiye report (Report 2025/26) documents the national enforcement climate that applies to provincial authorities in Gaziantep: in June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained; three activists were remanded in prison on 29 June 2025 under Law No. 2911 and released on 8 August pending trial, while prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. For Gaziantep this evidences the state-level hostility and case-by-case prosecutions under the same meeting-and-demonstrations law that a visibly trans visitor would face anywhere in Turkey, including this province.

Pride has been banned for a ninth consecutive year — 113 detained on 25 June 2023, 46 detained at the 2024 Acıbadem march with judicial controls and travel bans. sources.claim: Source covering this record’s claims: Kaos GL’s 2025 annual report (“The Year of the Family: A Major Siege Against LGBTI+ People”) documents state-policy hostility country-wide including Istanbul specifically — “especially in Istanbul, intensified practices of sealing or closing homes” obstructing access to housing. Its monitoring also records six violations of the right to life (three recorded as hate-motivated), trans people the most affected, torture and ill-treatment violations nearly doubled (89, up from 51), an LGBTI+ association closed with criminal cases against 11 members, and the state keeping no official hate-crime statistics.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (nav-only cache); the underlying news report covers the 31 July 2025 roundup of around 20 trans women in this city's Beyoğlu district for ID checks — names recorded, videos taken, 'this is profiling'.

Wikipedia's 'Istanbul Pride' article documents that since 2015 İstanbul pride parades have been denied permission and locally banned by the Governorship of İstanbul on security-and-public-order grounds (2016-2018 bans explicitly, water cannon used on 29 June 2015), and that 2014 was the biggest LGBT event in Turkey's history with over 100,000 participants. It records the escalating police suppression with numbers: blockades and tear gas in 2021 with 25 arrested; 373 arrested in 2022 with public transport to Taksim Square shut down; 113 arrests in 2023; and 11 arrests in 2024 (three of them minors) after organisers moved Istanbul Pride to non-Taksim public spaces and issued fake meeting calls to thwart police. This frames the record's 'banned for a ninth consecutive year' claim with a per-year detention tally a visitor can weigh.

Duvar English (27 June 2022) reports that on 26 June 2022 riot police dispersed the Pride march in İstanbul's Taksim Square, blockaded streets in the nearby Cihangir neighbourhood, shut down public transport to the square, and detained 373 people - including AFP photojournalist Bülent Kılıç - who were released after a night in custody, according to Kaos GL. The district governor's offices of Kadıköy and Beyoğlu in İstanbul had banned all LGBTI+ Pride Week events for seven days, and eight more people were detained at a Pride march in İzmir. The piece states Pride has been banned by Turkish authorities since 2014 and that police crackdowns on the parades have grown harsher over the years.

Mülteci-Der's report on Syrian trans women living here found they cannot find work, face exploitation and harassment when they do, and have 'no faith in justice'. sources.claim: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025) reports a leaked draft of Türkiye's omnibus '11th Judicial Package' (national framework; the record's national-frame claim on the draft rests on this) that would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed contrary to biological sex and general morality and its promotion with up to three years' prison, and participation in same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies with up to four years, and would amend civil code article 40 to raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care including surgery from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility and repeated evaluations at government-approved hospitals. Healthcare professionals performing deemed-illegal interventions would face fines and up to seven years' prison and trans people receiving such care up to three years, with courts able to order pretrial detention; fifteen Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed the draft, and HRW warns it would force treatment into unregulated underground settings.

Kaos GL's report on 2025 ('A Major Siege against LGBTI+ People in 2025: Hostility Turned into State Policy'; national framework, backing the record's national-frame claims) finds hostility toward LGBTI+ people became explicit state policy: for the first time in many years an LGBTI+ association was closed and criminal cases were opened against 11 of its members for human rights advocacy. It documents six right-to-life violations, three recorded as hate-motivated killings with trans people the most affected, 89 torture/ill-treatment violations, and 313 violations of the right to liberty in 2025 — roughly two and a half times the previous year — citing detentions, arrests and criminal cases against Pride participants as main reasons.
